## Module 5 at a glance {#module-5-overview}

**What you will do.** You compare your study samples with a reference set of people from known world regions. You calculate a few numbers for each person that describe their genetic background. You then remove the few samples whose background is very different from the rest.

**What you will learn.**

- Why differences in [ancestry](../docs/glossary.md#ancestry) between cases and controls can create false results.
- How a [principal component](../docs/glossary.md#pca-pc) (PC) summarises genetic variation in one number per person.
- How to place study samples on reference axes and draw them in a plot.
- How to flag ancestry outliers with one fixed rule.
- How to choose and justify the number of PCs for the later analysis.

**How long it takes.** About 60 minutes. The slowest step is 5.4, which runs PLINK three times.

## 5.1 Why ancestry matters {#step-5-1}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "This supplied subset has 1,062 samples labelled EUR, AFR, EAS and SAS.", "student_summary": "We count the reference samples in each labelled group. These groups help us compare inherited genetic backgrounds and understand how differences between cases and controls can create false disease associations.", "student_plink_options": []} -->
### What we do

Learn how [population structure](../docs/glossary.md#population-stratification) can mislead an association study. Then look at the reference samples we will use.

### Why

Cases and controls may be recruited from groups with different ancestry. Ancestry means the broad genetic background that a person inherits from their forebears. Then the [allele frequency](../docs/glossary.md#allele-frequency) (how common an allele is in a group) can differ between cases and controls, even at sites that have nothing to do with the disease. This is called [confounding](../docs/glossary.md#confounding): a hidden factor is associated with both the group and the genetics.

A principal component (PC) is a single number per person that summarises one main direction of genetic variation across many sites. Principal component analysis (PCA) is the method that finds these directions. PCA only describes patterns. Its axes are not diagnoses, nationality or ethnicity. The reference labels are background information, not a ranking of people. We define an ancestry-matched teaching cohort before we look at any association p-values.

### You need

The saved state from the end of module 4. You also need the supplied GRCh38 [reference subset](../docs/glossary.md#reference-subset), which comes with the course package.

### Command

```{r s5-1}
# 1. Read the reference sample table.
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
reference_samples <- guided_table(paste0(reference, ".psam"))
# 2. Count the samples in each reference group.
table(reference_samples$SuperPop)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

### Quick check

Can an allele-frequency difference between cases and controls appear because their ancestry differs, even when the site has no effect on the disease?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

Yes. Ancestry can influence both which group a person is in and which alleles that person carries.

</details>

### Files created

<details><summary>Optional: deep dives</summary>

These optional boxes are not part of the main path. No later step uses them. They write no file in your results folder. They are four deep dives on principal components: what a component is, why genetic data form clusters, where mixed people lie, and genes and geography.

#### Deep dive: what is a principal component?

**Why we use simulations.** The examples in this course use simulated data. In simulated data we know the truth: which populations exist, where each person comes from and which effects are real. So we can check whether a method finds the truth, and see when it fails. In real data we never know the truth for sure.

**Why this simulation.** A principal component (PC) is a direction. This example shows how PCA finds it for two measurements.

**How to read the chart.** Each dot is a person, with height across and arm span up, each minus the average. The thick line is a direction that you choose. Grey lines drop each dot onto it. The table gives the variance of the dropped dots, their spread along the line.

{{example:pc-rotation}}

**Try this.**

- Move the **Angle of the line (degrees)** slider to **0**. The line ignores arm span and holds little of the spread.
- Move it to **45**. The line follows the long direction of the cloud. The share is large.
- Move it to **135**. The line cuts across the cloud. The share is small.

**What you should see, and why.** Height and arm span rise together, so the cloud is long in one direction. The variance is largest there. That direction is PC1, and the table gives its angle. PC2 is at a right angle to it. With genotypes, each variant is one measurement, and a person's number along a direction is the score.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** [Step 5.4](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-4) turns thousands of variants into a few scores per person. [Step 6.2](module_06_association.Rmd#step-6-2) uses the scores as [covariates](../docs/glossary.md#covariate).

**Key idea:** A PC is the direction of largest spread, and the data choose it.

**R code.** Change `angle` at the top of the chunk and run it again.

```{r s5-1_dd_rotation, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. Nothing here changes your results folder.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
# Change this angle (in degrees) and run the chunk again.
angle <- 20
data <- demo_rotation_data()
angles <- c(angle, 0, 45, 90, 135)
frames <- lapply(angles, function(a) demo_rotation_frame(data, a))
# Title of each panel: the angle and the share of the total variance on the line.
titles <- sprintf("%d degrees: %.0f%%", angles, 100 * vapply(frames, function(f) f$stats$share, numeric(1)))
demo_plot_panels(frames, titles, "People", "Height (cm, centred)", "Arm span (cm, centred)", equal = TRUE)
# The angle of PC1, found by PCA.
demo_rotation_pc1_angle(data)
```
**Quick check.** Can a turned line ever hold more variance than PC1?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. PC1 is defined as the direction with the largest variance. Every other direction holds the same or less.

</details>

**Reference.** Jolliffe IT, Cadima J. 2016. Principal component analysis: a review and recent developments. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 374:20150202. [doi:10.1098/rsta.2015.0202](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.2015.0202).

#### Deep dive: why genetic data form clusters

**Why this simulation.** Two populations do not always form two clusters. When does PCA show them?

**How to read the chart.** Each dot is a person: circles are population A, triangles are population B. Fst is how different their allele frequencies are (0 means identical). The table gives the separation of A and B on PC1: above 3 is a clear gap. The mark on the Fst slider is the threshold of Patterson et al. 2006: 1 divided by the square root of the people times the variants.

{{example:fst-snps}}

**Try this.**

- Move the **Fst** slider to **0.001** and the **Number of variants** slider to **1000**. The groups mix.
- Move the **Number of variants** slider to **100000**. The mark falls below your Fst, and the groups separate.
- Move the **Fst** slider to **0**. They mix again.

**What you should see, and why.** Each variant differs a little between the populations, and PCA adds these differences up. The groups separate when the Fst is above the mark. More people or variants lower the mark. Near it, the result varies.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** In [step 5.5](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-5) you look for clusters. One cloud does not prove one ancestry: there may be too little data.

**Key idea:** PCA shows two populations apart only when the Fst, the people and the variants are large enough together.

**R code.** Change `fst` and run the chunk again.

```{r s5-1_dd_fst, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. This takes about ten seconds.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
# Change this value (0, 0.0005, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01 or 0.05) and run the chunk again.
fst <- 0.005
snps <- c(1000, 10000, 100000)
frames <- demo_fst_frames(fst, snps, seed = 1)
demo_plot_panels(frames, paste(format(snps, big.mark = ","), "variants"), c("Population A", "Population B"))
# Separation of A and B on PC1: 0 means no separation, and a value above 3 is a clear gap.
round(vapply(frames, function(f) f$stats$separation, numeric(1)), 2)
# The Fst at the phase change for each number of variants: 1 divided by the square root of (people times variants).
signif(vapply(frames, function(f) f$stats$threshold, numeric(1)), 2)
```
**Quick check.** A study has few variants. PCA shows one cloud for two closely related populations. Does this prove that the populations are the same?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. With this amount of data, a small difference cannot be seen. More people or more variants could show two clusters.

</details>

**Reference.** Patterson N, Price AL, Reich D. 2006. Population structure and eigenanalysis. PLoS Genetics 2:e190. [doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.0020190](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0020190).

#### Deep dive: where do mixed people lie?

**Why this simulation.** Some people have ancestors from two populations. This example shows where PCA puts them.

**How to read the chart.** Circles are population A, triangles B and squares C. Diamonds are 40 mixed people from A and B. The table gives their mean position on the line from A (0) to B (1), and the position expected from their ancestry.

{{example:admixture}}

**Try this.**

- Move the **Share of ancestry from A in the mixed people** slider to **0.5**. The diamonds lie half-way between A and B.
- Move it to **0.9**. They move towards A.
- Move it to **0.1**. They move towards B.

**What you should see, and why.** The allele frequencies of a mixed person are a blend of A and B. PCA uses allele counts, so the person lies between the two sources. Population C is not in the mix, so it lies elsewhere.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** In [step 5.6](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-6) you keep people close to the European group. A mixed person lies between groups, and the distance shows how far from Europeans.

**Key idea:** A mixed person lies between the source populations, in proportion to the mix.

**R code.** Change `shares` and run the chunk again.

```{r s5-1_dd_admixture, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. Each frame takes a few seconds.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
# Change these shares of ancestry from A in the mixed people and run the chunk again.
shares <- c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9)
frames <- lapply(shares, function(s) demo_admixture_frame(s, seed = 1))
demo_plot_panels(frames, paste("Share from A:", shares), c("A", "B", "C", "Mixed A and B"))
```
**Quick check.** A person lies half-way between A and B on the plot. Give one reason, other than admixture, that could place a person there.

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

A person from a third population that is genetically between A and B, but was not sampled, can lie there too. A technical problem with the genotypes can also move a person. A position alone does not show the ancestry.

</details>

#### Deep dive: genes and geography

Novembre et al. 2008 ([doi:10.1038/nature07331](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature07331)) found that PC1 and PC2 of 1,387 Europeans look like a map of Europe, once the axes are turned by 16 degrees. They warn that the axes depend on how samples are spread. Novembre and Stephens 2008 ([doi:10.1038/ng.139](https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.139)) show that smooth gradients give wave-like patterns that need not show migrations. This example is our own.

**Why this simulation.** Do genes mirror geography? When does PCA draw a map of populations?

**How to read the chart.** Labels A1 to F6 are the mean positions of 36 populations on a 6 by 6 grid. Lines join neighbours, and small dots are people. The table gives the mean position error in grid steps. Raw PCA has no north, so the turned view uses Procrustes analysis to turn, flip and scale the plot onto the true grid.

{{example:stepping-stone}}

**Try this.**

- Move the **View** slider to **Turned onto the true grid (Procrustes)** and the **Migration rate between neighbours** slider to **0.25**. The grid is recovered.
- Move the **Migration rate between neighbours** slider to **0.8**. The grid blurs. Move it to **0.01**. The populations become islands.
- Move the **Migration rate between neighbours** slider to **0.25** and the **Sampling** slider to **Corner: many people in A1, B1, A2 and B2**. The sampled corner takes more room.

**What you should see, and why.** With moderate migration, nearby populations share ancestry and lie close, so the grid appears. With very high migration all populations are alike. With very low migration each is an island. PCA has no north, so we turn the plot ourselves. Who is sampled changes the shape.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** In [step 5.5](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-5) a gradient in your cohort can look like clusters or a map. The PCs used as covariates in [step 5.7](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-7) capture such gradients. Do not read plot shapes as migration history.

**Key idea:** PCA can draw a map of populations, but only when migration and sampling allow it, and we choose its direction.

**R code.** Change `migration` and run the chunk again.

```{r s5-1_dd_grid, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. Nothing here changes your results folder.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
# Change this migration rate (try 0.8, 0.25, 0.1 or 0.01) and run the chunk again.
migration <- 0.25
uniform <- demo_stepping_stone(migration, "uniform")
corner <- demo_stepping_stone(migration, "corner")
frames <- list(demo_stepping_frame(uniform, turned = FALSE), demo_stepping_frame(uniform, turned = TRUE),
               demo_stepping_frame(corner, turned = TRUE))
demo_plot_panels(frames, c("Raw PCA, uniform sampling", "Turned onto the grid, uniform sampling", "Turned onto the grid, corner sampling"),
                 equal = TRUE, xlab = "East-west (grid steps)", ylab = "North-south (grid steps)")
# Mean error of the population positions, in grid steps: raw, turned, turned with corner sampling.
round(c(uniform$error_raw, uniform$error_turned, corner$error_turned), 2)
```
**Quick check.** Can we say that PC1 points north?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. PCA chooses its axes by variance, not by geography. The sign and the angle depend on the sample. We turned the plot ourselves, using the true grid.

</details>

</details>

## 5.2 Prepare variants for reference PCA {#step-5-2}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "48,615 shared sites are kept for the reference PCA and the projection.", "student_summary": "We find and save the 48,615 sites present in both the cleaned study and the reference. We need the same sites to compare genetic patterns in the two groups.", "student_plink_options": []} -->
### What we do

Find the sites that are present in both the reference subset and the cleaned study. Only common sites on the [autosomes](../docs/glossary.md#autosome) (chromosomes 1 to 22) are used.

### Why

Nearby sites are often inherited together, so they carry the same information. This is called linkage disequilibrium ([LD](../docs/glossary.md#ld)). If PCA uses many such sites, one long correlated stretch can dominate the result. To avoid this, the supplied reference was built with [LD pruning](../docs/glossary.md#ld-pruning), which keeps one site from each correlated group. It kept only common autosomal array sites. It used an [r^2](../docs/glossary.md#r-squared) limit of 0.15 in windows of 200 kb, and it kept at most 50,000 sites.

We keep only the sites that are in both the reference and the study after quality control (QC). We do not add back sites that failed earlier checks. We will prune the sites again later, after we define the final cohort.

### You need

The saved state from step 4.6, and the reference subset supplied at step 0.5.

### Command

```{r s5-2}
# 1. Read the study and reference site tables.
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
study_sites <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "4.6"), ".pvar"))
reference_sites <- guided_table(paste0(reference, ".pvar"))
# 2. Find the site names that occur in both tables.
common <- sort(intersect(study_sites$ID, reference_sites$ID))
# 3. Save the shared site names and check their number.
guided_list(common, guided_path(cfg, "5.2", "common.txt"))
stopifnot(length(common) == 48615L)
cat(length(common), "shared autosomal sites kept\n")
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "5.2", guided_path(cfg, "5.2", "common.txt"), parent = "4.6")
```

## 5.3 Match build, position and alleles {#step-5-3}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "All 48,615 shared IDs agree on chromosome, GRCh38 position and allele pair.", "student_summary": "We check that each shared site has the same chromosome, DNA position and the two DNA letters that can occur at that site, in both files. This prevents us from comparing different sites that happen to share a name.", "student_plink_options": []} -->
### What we do

Check that the shared variants are really the same variants in both files, before the projection.

### Why

Two variants with the same [rsID](../docs/glossary.md#rsid) (a public name for a variant) are not always the same variant. For each shared variant, check four things: the genome build, the chromosome, the position and the pair of [alleles](../docs/glossary.md#allele). In step 4.5 the array-style names were replaced by IDs made of position and alleles.

If two files list the same two alleles in a different order, the variant is still compatible. If the allele pair differs, or the DNA strand is not resolved, we cannot accept the match without checking. The projection uses the named allele in each weight. It does not use the order of rows in the two files.

### You need

The list of common sites from step 5.2, and the two variant tables (the `.pvar` files) of the study and the reference.

### Command

```{r s5-3}
# 1. Read the shared site names and both site tables.
common <- readLines(guided_path(cfg, "5.2", "common.txt"))
study <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "4.6"), ".pvar"))
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
ref <- guided_table(paste0(reference, ".pvar"))
# 2. Match site names and compare allele pairs in either order.
a <- match(common, study$ID); b <- match(common, ref$ID)
pair <- function(a, b) ifelse(a < b, paste0(a, b), paste0(b, a))
# 3. Check chromosomes, positions and alleles and print the matched count.
stopifnot(all(sub("^chr", "", study$CHROM[a]) == sub("^chr", "", ref$CHROM[b])),
  all(study$POS[a] == ref$POS[b]), all(pair(study$REF[a], study$ALT[a]) == pair(ref$REF[b], ref$ALT[b])))
cat("All", length(common), "shared sites agree on chromosome, position and alleles\n")
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable: this step needs no PLINK command. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the displayed values without changing the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

All 48,615 shared IDs agree on chromosome, GRCh38 position and allele pair. This checks that the two supplied files are compatible. It is not an independent check against a reference genome sequence file (a FASTA file).

<!-- verification_note:start -->The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks and the expected counts passed on Windows.<!-- verification_note:end -->

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error message. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

"--out", "explanation": "Starts the study score output file names with s5-4_study_scores."}]}]} -->
### What we do

Calculate the PCs in the reference only. Then place the reference samples and the study samples on the same axes.

### Why

If we ran one PCA on reference and study together, a much larger study group could pull the axes towards itself. So we fix the axes on the reference first. Placing new samples on fixed axes is called [projection](../docs/glossary.md#projection).

Each site has an allele weight (called a loading), which says how much that allele contributes to a PC. The score of a person is the sum of these weights over the alleles the person carries. The reference and the study scores must use the same allele frequencies, the same weights and the same standardisation. Standardisation means rescaling each genotype by the allele frequency, so that common and rare alleles count fairly. The scale and the sign (plus or minus) of a PC are arbitrary. Compare patterns only when both sets of scores use the same scale.

The weight file names the counted allele in a column called [A1](../docs/glossary.md#a1). We switch off mean imputation. This means a missing call is not replaced by the average, so the missing calls stay visible in the score.

### You need

The checked shared sites from step 5.3, and the full saved state from step 4.6.

### Command

```{r s5-4}
# 1. Set the reference input, shared site list and output names.
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
common <- guided_path(cfg, "5.2", "common.txt")
fit <- guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "reference")
# 2. Calculate ten reference components and save their allele contributions.
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", reference, "--extract", common, "--freq", "--pca", "10", "allele-wts", "--out", fit))
# 3. Find the columns containing site names, alleles and component contributions.
weights <- guided_table(paste0(fit, ".eigenvec.allele"))
id_column <- match("ID", names(weights)); allele_column <- match("A1", names(weights))
first_pc <- match("PC1", names(weights))
# 4. Prepare the same reference frequencies and scoring rules for both groups.
score <- c("--read-freq", paste0(fit, ".afreq"), "--score", paste0(fit, ".eigenvec.allele"),
  id_column, allele_column, "header-read", "no-mean-imputation", "variance-standardize",
  "--score-col-nums", paste0(first_pc, "-", first_pc + 9L))
# 5. Place the reference samples on the fixed reference axes.
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", reference, "--extract", common, score, "--out", guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores")))
# 6. Place the study samples on the same reference axes.
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "4.6"), "--extract", common, score, "--out", guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores")))
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "5.4", c(paste0(fit, c(".afreq", ".eigenvec", ".eigenval", ".eigenvec.allele")), paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores"), ".sscore"), paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores"), ".sscore")), parent = "5.2")
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile data/course/pca_reference/ref1000g_grch38 --extract results/guided/s5-2_common.txt --freq --pca 10 allele-wts --out results/guided/s5-4_reference --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile data/course/pca_reference/ref1000g_grch38 --extract results/guided/s5-2_common.txt --read-freq results/guided/s5-4_reference.afreq --score results/guided/s5-4_reference.eigenvec.allele 2 5 header-read no-mean-imputation variance-standardize --score-col-nums 6-15 --out results/guided/s5-4_ref_scores --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s4-6_state --extract results/guided/s5-2_common.txt --read-freq results/guided/s5-4_reference.afreq --score results/guided/s5-4_reference.eigenvec.allele 2 5 header-read no-mean-imputation variance-standardize --score-col-nums 6-15 --out results/guided/s5-4_study_scores --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--extract` keeps only the checked shared sites. `--freq` writes the allele frequencies of the reference. `--pca 10 allele-wts` computes ten axes and saves the allele weights. `--read-freq` gives the same frequencies to both projections. `--score` names the weight file and the columns that hold the variant ID and the A1 allele (columns 2 and 5 here, counted from one). `header-read` tells PLINK to use the header line of the weight file. `no-mean-imputation` stops PLINK replacing missing calls with the average. `variance-standardize` scales the genotypes with the allele frequencies. `--score-col-nums 6-15` selects PC1 to PC10. The R command finds these column numbers from the real header line. `--pfile` reads the named genotype files in PLINK 2 format. `--out` sets the name of the output files. `--threads 2` limits the number of worker threads. `--memory 2048` sets the working memory to 2048 MiB.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

Reference eigenvectors and eigenvalues, allele weights, and two `.sscore` files (score tables) with the columns PC1_AVG to PC10_AVG. The study projection contains 1,844 samples.

<details><summary>Optional: deep dives</summary>

This optional box is not part of the main path. No later step uses it. It writes no file in your results folder. These examples use simulated data, so the true answer is known. The first box of [step 5.1](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-1) explains why.

#### Deep dive: what does projecting mean, and why do projected people shrink?

**Why this simulation.** In step 5.4 study people are placed on axes made from a reference. This example asks whether the placement keeps the distances.

**How to read the chart.** Circles and triangles are reference people (populations A and B). Squares and diamonds are study people. The study does not make the axes. The table gives the gap between the study groups on PC1 divided by the gap in the reference: 1 means no shrinkage, which is the pull of study people towards the centre.

{{example:projection}}

**Try this.**

- Move the **Reference people in each population** slider to **10** and the **Fst** slider to **0.01**. The study dots huddle near the centre.
- Move the **Reference people in each population** slider to **400**. The study dots spread out to match the reference.
- Move the **Fst** slider to **0.002**. The study dots move towards the centre again.

**What you should see, and why.** The axes are fitted to the reference people, noise included. Study people are not fitted, so they lie nearer the centre. A larger reference has less noise to fit, and more different populations give a stronger signal.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** [Step 5.4](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-4) projects your study on 1000 Genomes axes. [Step 5.6](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-6) uses the first four PCs to find outliers. Privé et al. 2020 report that shrinkage is large only from PC5 on.

**Key idea:** Projected people are pulled towards the centre, more so when the reference is small.

**R code.** Change `n_ref` and run the chunk again.

```{r s5-4_dd_projection, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. Nothing here changes your results folder. This takes about ten seconds.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
# Change this number of reference people in each population (try 10, 25, 100 or 400).
n_ref <- 25
sizes <- c(n_ref, 10, 100, 400)
frames <- lapply(sizes, function(n) demo_projection_frame(n, fst = 0.01))
demo_plot_panels(frames, paste(sizes, "reference people per population"),
                 c("Reference, A", "Reference, B", "Study, A", "Study, B"))
# Shrinkage: the gap between the study groups divided by the gap between the reference groups. 1 means none.
round(vapply(frames, function(f) f$stats$ratio, numeric(1)), 2)
```
**Quick check.** Why can the reference people not show shrinkage themselves?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

The axes were fitted to them, noise included. Their positions are the fitted values. New people are not fitted, so they lack this advantage.

</details>

**Reference.** Privé et al. 2020 ([doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa520](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa520)) report a shrinkage bias of projected PCs, and they show how to obtain unbiased projections with the R package bigsnpr.

</details>

<details><summary>Under the hood & literature</summary>

**What the tool computes.** `--pca 10 allele-wts` finds the top ten principal components of the reference genotypes after each variant is shifted to mean 0 and scaled to variance 1 with its allele frequency. The `.eigenvec.allele` file has one line per allele. After the variant ID and `A1`, each `PC` column is the weight of that allele on that component. `--score` then gives each person the average of weight times standardised genotype over the shared alleles. The `_AVG` columns are averages, so their scale differs from the `.eigenvec` file. Use the projected scores for both groups.

**Why these values.** Ten components is PLINK's default and a course convention. Step 5.7 fixes how many enter the model. `--read-freq` gives both groups the same frequencies. `no-mean-imputation` leaves missing calls out of the average.

**Pitfalls.** Projected study samples shrink towards the origin, and the bias grows from PC5 onwards, so read distances on later PCs with care. An allele that does not match by name contributes nothing, so the score silently uses fewer sites. At an A/T or C/G site, a strand flip keeps the name but reverses the meaning and flips the sign of its contribution. This is why the shared sites are checked at step 5.3. A person from an ancestry absent from the reference tends to land near the closest reference group. The spelling `variance-standardize` is American; the course text says standardise.

**References**

1. Patterson N et al. (2006) Population structure and eigenanalysis. PLoS Genet 2:e190. PMID 17194218.
2. Price AL et al. (2006) Principal components analysis corrects for stratification in genome-wide association studies. Nat Genet 38:904-909. PMID 16862161.
3. Privé F et al. (2020) Efficient toolkit implementing best practices for principal component analysis of population genetic data. Bioinformatics 36:4449-4457. PMID 32415959.
4. The 1000 Genomes Project Consortium (2015) A global reference for human genetic variation. Nature 526:68-74. PMID 26432245.

</details>

## 5.5 Plot the reference and projected study {#step-5-5}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "A labelled plot of the reference with the projected study.", "student_summary": "We plot the first three principal components, each a number summarising one pattern of genetic variation, in three pairs. We show reference groups with labels and symbols and add the study samples to see how their genetic backgrounds compare.", "student_plink_options": []} -->
### What we do

Draw three plots of the first three reference axes: PC1 against PC2, PC1 against PC3 and PC2 against PC3. Each reference group has its own label and symbol, and the study samples are added on top. All three plots use the same symbols, colours and key.

### Why

A plot of two PCs helps us see large differences between samples. Later PCs can show patterns that PC1 and PC2 hide. This is why we also plot PC3 against each of the first two. A difference can also come from the genotyping platform, from missing data or from allele errors. The study points are projected scores. They are not a separate PCA. The groups use symbols as well as colour, so the plot stays readable without colour.

### You need

The score files from step 5.4, and the reference sample table.

### Command

```{r s5-5}
# 1. Read both score tables and the reference group labels.
ref <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores"), ".sscore"))
study <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores"), ".sscore"))
metadata <- guided_table(file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38.psam"))
# 2. Match the reference labels to samples and choose group symbols and colours.
group <- metadata$SuperPop[match(ref$IID, metadata$IID)]
levels <- sort(unique(group)); code <- match(group, levels)
colours <- c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73", "#CC79A7", "#E69F00")
# 3. Define one plotting function, so that all pictures use the same symbols, colours and key.
plot_components <- function(x, y, file) {
  png(file, width = 1400, height = 850, res = 140)
  par(mar = c(5, 4.5, 4, 9))
  plot(as.numeric(ref[[paste0("PC", x, "_AVG")]]), as.numeric(ref[[paste0("PC", y, "_AVG")]]), col = colours[code], pch = code,
    xlab = paste0("Reference PC", x, " score"), ylab = paste0("Reference PC", y, " score"),
    main = paste0("GRCh38 reference and projected simulated study: PC", x, " and PC", y))
  # Add the study samples and a key for the groups. The key sits outside the plot, on the right, so it hides no points.
  points(as.numeric(study[[paste0("PC", x, "_AVG")]]), as.numeric(study[[paste0("PC", y, "_AVG")]]), pch = 20, cex = 0.4, col = "#333333")
  legend("topright", inset = c(-0.21, 0), xpd = TRUE, legend = c(levels, "Study projection"), col = c(colours[seq_along(levels)], "#333333"), pch = c(seq_along(levels), 20), cex = 0.8)
  invisible(dev.off())
}
# 4. Save the picture for PC1 and PC2, then the two extra pictures for PC1 and PC3 and for PC2 and PC3.
files <- c(guided_path(cfg, "5.5", "reference_projection.png"),
  guided_path(cfg, "5.5", "reference_projection_pc1_pc3.png"),
  guided_path(cfg, "5.5", "reference_projection_pc2_pc3.png"))
plot_components(1, 2, files[1]); plot_components(1, 3, files[2]); plot_components(2, 3, files[3])
# 5. Print the location of each picture.
for (file in files) cat("The plot was saved to ", file, "\n", sep = "")
```

### Optional: a 3D plot with ellipses

<details><summary>Show the optional 3D plot</summary>

This box is not part of the main path. No later step uses it. The code is not run by default. It draws the three first components in one rotating 3D picture. A 95% ellipse is drawn around each reference group. An ellipse shows where about 95% of the points of a group are expected to lie. The code needs the package `rgl`, which step 0.5 does not install. To install it once, type `install.packages("rgl")` in the R console. On macOS, `rgl` may also need the free program XQuartz. If the package does not install, or no window opens, skip this box. The code does nothing when `rgl` is missing.

```{r s5-5_optional_3d, eval=FALSE}
# Optional. Needs the rgl package: install.packages("rgl")
if (requireNamespace("rgl", quietly = TRUE)) {
  # 1. Collect the scores of the first three components for the reference samples.
  scores <- cbind(as.numeric(ref$PC1_AVG), as.numeric(ref$PC2_AVG), as.numeric(ref$PC3_AVG))
  # 2. Draw the reference samples in 3D, with the colours used in the 2D plots.
  rgl::plot3d(scores, col = colours[code], size = 4, xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2", zlab = "PC3")
  # 3. Add one 95% ellipse for each reference group.
  for (i in seq_along(levels)) {
    group_scores <- scores[code == i, , drop = FALSE]
    rgl::plot3d(rgl::ellipse3d(cov(group_scores), centre = colMeans(group_scores), level = 0.95),
      col = colours[i], alpha = 0.15, add = TRUE)
  }
} else {
  message("The rgl package is not installed. Skip this optional plot.")
}
```

</details>

<details><summary>Optional: deep dives</summary>

These optional boxes are not part of the main path. No later step uses them. They write only files that start with `s5-5_dd_`. The examples use simulated data, so the true answer is known. The first box of [step 5.1](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-1) explains why. They are four deep dives: what a PCA plot is not, a real example with European populations, the colour model, and a debate about what a PCA plot tells us.

#### Deep dive: what a PCA plot is not

**Why this simulation.** Are PCA axes a property of populations, or of the sample? Here the sample changes and the populations do not.

**How to read the chart.** Circles are population A, triangles B, 200 people in all. The centre is the mean of the sample. The table gives the first eigenvalue (the variance along PC1) and the mean PC1 score of each population.

{{example:composition}}

**Try this.**

- Move the **Share of the sample from B** slider to **0.5**. The two populations lie on opposite sides of the centre.
- Move it to **0.9**. The small group A lies far from the centre, and B lies near it.
- Move it to **0.1**. The positions swap.

**What you should see, and why.** The larger population lies near the centre, because the centre is the sample mean. The first eigenvalue is largest when the sizes are equal. The populations did not change. Only the sample did.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** The PCs of [step 5.7](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-7) summarise your final cohort. If you add or remove many people, they change, so the course fixes the cohort first.

**Key idea:** A PCA plot describes the sample you give it, so the axes change when the sample changes.

**R code.** Change `share_b` and run the chunk again.

```{r s5-5_dd_composition, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. Nothing here changes your results folder. This takes about ten seconds.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
# Change this share of the sample that comes from population B (the other panels use fixed shares).
share_b <- 0.1
shares <- c(share_b, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9)
frames <- lapply(shares, function(s) demo_composition_frame(s, seed = 4000))
demo_plot_panels(frames, paste0(shares * 100, "% from B"), c("Population A", "Population B"))
# First eigenvalue and mean PC1 score of each population, for each share.
round(t(vapply(frames, function(f) unlist(f$stats[c("eigenvalue", "mean_a", "mean_b")]), numeric(3))), 3)
```
**Quick check.** A study doubles the number of people from one population. Does PC1 describe the same difference as before?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

The difference between the populations is the same, but the axes, the eigenvalues and the distances on the plot change. A plot is a summary of one sample. It is not a measurement of the populations.

</details>

**What a cluster is.** A cluster is a summary of allele frequencies, not a sharp biological category. We say genetic ancestry or ancestry group, not race or ethnicity.

**Reference.** McVean G. 2009. A genealogical interpretation of principal components analysis. PLoS Genetics 5:e1000686. [doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1000686](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1000686).

#### Deep dive: a real example with European populations

**The idea.** The examples above use simulated data. The reference of step 5.4 holds real people from the 1000 Genomes project. Some of them come from European populations: GBR (British), CEU (Utah residents with northern and western European ancestry), FIN (Finnish), IBS (Iberian) and TSI (Tuscan). The code keeps these people and calculates new PCs with only them. It uses the shared sites of step 5.2 and common variants. The table printed by the first line shows which of the five populations your reference holds. The step writes only files that start with `s5-5_dd_eur`.

```{r s5-5_dd_eur, eval=FALSE}
# Optional. This takes about ten seconds. It writes only files that start with s5-5_dd_eur.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
psam <- read.delim(paste0(reference, ".psam"), check.names = FALSE)
# 1. Keep the people of the European populations that the reference holds.
wanted <- c("GBR", "CEU", "FIN", "IBS", "TSI")
people <- psam[psam$Population %in% wanted, c("#IID", "Population")]
table(people$Population)
keep <- guided_path(cfg, "5.5", "dd_eur_keep.txt")
write.table(data.frame(IID = people[["#IID"]]), keep, quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, sep = "\t")
# 2. Calculate four PCs with only these people. PLINK needs common variants for this (--maf 0.05).
fit <- guided_path(cfg, "5.5", "dd_eur")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", reference, "--extract", guided_path(cfg, "5.2", "common.txt"), "--keep", keep,
                 "--maf", "0.05", "--freq", "--pca", "4", "--out", fit), quiet = TRUE)
# 3. Plot PC1 against PC2. Each population has its own shape and colour.
pcs <- read.delim(paste0(fit, ".eigenvec"), check.names = FALSE)
names(pcs)[1] <- "IID"
pcs$Population <- people$Population[match(pcs$IID, people[["#IID"]])]
present <- intersect(wanted, unique(pcs$Population))
g <- match(pcs$Population, present)
plot(pcs$PC1, pcs$PC2, pch = demo_marks$shapes[g], col = demo_marks$colours[g], xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2",
     main = "European populations of the 1000 Genomes reference")
legend("topright", legend = present, pch = demo_marks$shapes[seq_along(present)], col = demo_marks$colours[seq_along(present)], bty = "n")
# 4. The mean position of each population.
aggregate(cbind(PC1, PC2) ~ Population, pcs, mean)
```

**What to observe.** Some populations overlap, and others lie apart. The positions follow the geography of the populations in a loose way, as in the study of Novembre et al. 2008 ([doi:10.1038/nature07331](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature07331)). The sign and the angle of the axes still depend on this sample. These PCs were calculated from European people only, so they are different from the PCs of step 5.4, which come from all the populations of the reference.

**Quick check.** Why do the PCs of this plot differ from the PCs of step 5.4?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

The PCs summarise the people who are in the sample. This sample holds only European people, so the PCs describe the differences among them. The sample of step 5.4 also holds people from other regions of the world, and the largest differences there are between regions.

</details>

#### Debate: the colour model

In 2022 Elhaik argued that PCA results can be artefacts of the data and can be manipulated ([doi:10.1038/s41598-022-14395-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-14395-4)). This box uses the idea of its colour model. The code is our own, and we reproduce no figure.

**Why this simulation.** Can the same data give different PCA pictures? Four colours stand for four populations.

**How to read the chart.** A person is three numbers, like three variants: Red (1,0,0), Green (0,1,0), Blue (0,0,1), Black (0,0,0), with a little noise. There are always 50 black people. Each dot is the mean position of a colour. The tables give true distances, distances over all three PCs and distances in the PC1-PC2 plane.

{{example:colour-model}}

**Try this.**

- Move the **Red people** slider to **50**, the **Green people** slider to **50** and the **Blue people** slider to **50**. Black is equally far from the three colours.
- Move the **Red people** slider to **25**. Black comes closer to Red.
- Move it to **100**. Black moves away from Red.

**What you should see, and why.** PCA rotates the data, so distances over all three PCs stay true. The plot keeps two PCs, so it distorts them, and the distortion depends on how many people each colour has. A colour with many people pushes Black away (Elhaik 2022).

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** Plots in [step 5.5](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-5) show two PCs out of many, so their distances are not true genetic distances. Use them to find outliers ([step 5.6](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-6)), not to measure relatedness.

**Key idea:** Keeping only two PCs distorts distances, and how much depends on who is in the sample.

**R code.** Change `n_red` and run the chunk again.

```{r s5-5_dd_colours, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. Nothing here changes your results folder.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
# Change this number of red people and run the chunk again (the other colours have 50 people each).
n_red <- 25
sizes <- c(n_red, 50, 100)
frames <- lapply(sizes, function(n) demo_colour_frame(n, 50, 50))
demo_plot_panels(frames, paste(sizes, "red people"), c("Red", "Green", "Blue", "Black"))
# Distance from Black to each colour: true, over all three PCs, and in the PC1-PC2 plane.
distances <- function(f) unlist(f$stats[c("true_red_black", "true_green_black", "true_blue_black",
                                          "all_red_black", "all_green_black", "all_blue_black",
                                          "plane_red_black", "plane_green_black", "plane_blue_black")])
result <- t(vapply(frames, distances, numeric(9)))
rownames(result) <- paste(sizes, "red people")
round(result, 2)
```
#### Debate: what does a PCA plot tell us?

**Why a debate.** How to read PCA plots of human genetic data is debated. This box separates what the colour model shows from the wider claims of the article.

- **What the model shows.** The plot depends on the sample. This is not new: Novembre et al. 2008, McVean 2009 and Novembre and Stephens 2008 all discuss how PCA patterns depend on sampling, space and ancestry.
- **The most far-reaching claim.** The article concludes that 32,000 to 216,000 genetic studies should be reevaluated. A model with three variants cannot show this. Judge it against independent replies. We cite none, because we could not verify one.
- **Two uses of PCA.** One tells a story about origins from a plot. The other uses PCs as covariates to remove confounding, and the article criticises it too. Test it on your data: step 5.7 shows lambda and hits for 0 to 20 PCs.

**Question 1.** Does PCA reconstruct geography, or do we choose it with the rotation?

<details><summary>Note for the instructor</summary>

Both. The structure is in the data, as in the grid example. The direction is not: Novembre et al. 2008 chose the angle that best matched latitude and longitude.

</details>

**Question 2.** What changes if we double the sample of one population?

<details><summary>Note for the instructor</summary>

The axes, eigenvalues and distances change, not the populations. Ask students to predict the plot first. In the colour example, a colour with fewer people comes closer to Black in the plane.

</details>

**Question 3.** Is a person between two clusters necessarily mixed?

<details><summary>Note for the instructor</summary>

No. The person may come from a third population, or from how the sample was chosen, or have a technical problem. Mixed ancestry needs other evidence.

</details>

**Question 4.** Why do these limits weigh less for association studies than for the history of populations?

<details><summary>Note for the instructor</summary>

A scan needs PCs that remove confounding, checked with lambda. It does not need the axes to tell a true story. The limits still matter: outliers can take over axes (step 5.6) and PCs of one region can bias results (Grinde et al. 2024).

</details>

**References.** Elhaik E. 2022. Scientific Reports 12:14683. [doi:10.1038/s41598-022-14395-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-14395-4). Novembre J, et al. 2008. [doi:10.1038/nature07331](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature07331). Novembre J, Stephens M. 2008. [doi:10.1038/ng.139](https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.139). McVean G. 2009. [doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1000686](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1000686).

</details>

## 5.6 Define an ancestry-matched cohort {#step-5-6}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "33 remaining outlier records are excluded. 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants remain.", "student_summary": "We compare each study sample with a European reference group on the first four principal components, numbers that summarise patterns of genetic variation. We remove a sample if any of them lies more than six standard deviations (a measure of spread) from the reference mean; this rule defines the group for our teaching analysis.", "student_plink_options": [{"label": "remove samples outside the reference rule", "options": [{"name": "--pfile", "explanation": "Reads the cleaned study genotype files s4-6_state.pgen, .pvar and .psam from the results folder."}, {"name": "--remove", "explanation": "Removes the samples listed in s5-6_remove.txt because at least one of their first four component scores is more than six standard deviations from the European reference mean."}, {"name": "--make-pgen", "explanation": "Saves the retained 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants as PGEN, PVAR and PSAM files."}, {"name": "--out", "explanation": "Starts the retained study output file names with s5-6_state."}]}]} -->
### What we do

Apply a rule, fixed in advance, to the first four projected PCs. The rule flags samples that are more than six standard deviations from the European reference.

### Why

In this teaching design, the main analysis uses a cohort that broadly matches the European reference. The rule has three parts. First, take the European reference samples. For each of PC1 to PC4, calculate their mean and their [standard deviation](../docs/glossary.md#standard-deviation) (a measure of how spread out the values are). Second, convert each study score into a distance from that mean, counted in standard deviations. Third, flag a sample as an [outlier](../docs/glossary.md#outlier) if its largest distance, ignoring the sign, is above six.

This is a rule for this study only. It is not a general way to classify ancestry. Apply it before you look at any association results, and report who was excluded.

### You need

The reference and study scores from step 5.4, and the reference labels used in step 5.5.

### Command

```{r s5-6}
# 1. Read the reference and study scores and reference group labels.
ref <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores"), ".sscore"))
study <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores"), ".sscore"))
metadata <- guided_table(file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38.psam"))
# 2. Select the European reference samples and the first four component scores.
eur <- metadata$SuperPop[match(ref$IID, metadata$IID)] == "EUR"
columns <- paste0("PC", 1:4, "_AVG")
r <- sapply(ref[eur, columns, drop = FALSE], as.numeric)
s <- sapply(study[columns], as.numeric)
# 3. Measure each study score's distance from the reference mean using its spread.
centre <- colMeans(r)
spread <- sqrt(colMeans(sweep(r, 2, centre, "-")^2))
z <- sweep(sweep(s, 2, centre, "-"), 2, spread, "/")
# 4. List samples more than six standard deviations away on any selected component.
bad <- study$IID[apply(abs(z), 1, max) > 6]
remove <- guided_list(bad, guided_path(cfg, "5.6", "remove.txt"), TRUE)
# 5. Remove the listed samples and save the retained study group.
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "4.6"), "--remove", remove, "--make-pgen", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "5.6")))
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
ops <- guided_replay_lists(cfg, "5.6", "4.6")
guided_register(cfg, "5.6", "5.4", 1811, 238513, operations = ops)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s4-6_state --remove results/guided/s5-6_remove.txt --make-pgen --out results/guided/s5-6_state --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

R applies the rule and writes the list of flagged sample IDs (IIDs). `--remove` takes out the samples on that list from the full study data. `--make-pgen` saves the retained cohort. `--pfile` reads the named genotype files in PLINK 2 format. `--out` sets the name of the output files. `--threads 2` limits the number of worker threads. `--memory 2048` sets the working memory to 2048 MiB.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

33 remaining outlier records are excluded. 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants remain. Some of the simulated outliers were already removed in earlier QC steps. So 33 is not the total number of outliers in the original data.

<!-- verification_note:start -->The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks and the expected counts passed on Windows.<!-- verification_note:end -->

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error message. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### What this check can reveal

Large differences in ancestry compared with the reference, and possible technical outliers. A mismatch needs a review and a written study design. It does not mean that the excluded people are unsuitable in general.

### Quick check

Why does the rule use four PCs and not only the two shown in the plot?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

A difference that is weak or invisible on the first two axes can appear on later axes.

</details>

### Files created

`s5-6_remove.txt`, `s5-6_state.*` and replay metadata.

<details><summary>Try other thresholds (optional)</summary>
This optional box is not part of the main path and does not change your results. The examples use simulated data, so the true answer is known ([why](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-1)).

Each trial starts from the study samples of step 4.6.

**Chart: SD limit.**

**Why this simulation.** Step 5.6 removes people far from the European reference. How many standard deviations (SD) is far?

**How to read the chart.** Each point is one SD limit. A person is removed when they are farther than that many SD from the European mean on any of the first four PCs. The vertical axis counts the people removed, and the diamond marks the course value.

**Try this.**

- Move the slider to **4**. One more person is removed.
- Move it to **8**. The count equals the course value.

**What you should see, and why.** The real outliers are far from the European group, so any sensible limit finds them. Only the strictest limit adds a person.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** [step 5.6](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-6) defines your ancestry-matched cohort. The limit hardly changes who is removed, so you can fix it before you see association results.

**Key idea:** Real outliers are far away, so the exact SD limit changes little.

**Chart: MCD chi-squared quantile.**

**Why this simulation.** Another method uses a robust distance. How does its cutoff change who is removed?

**How to read the chart.** Each point is one cutoff of the robust Mahalanobis distance, given as a chi-squared quantile (a probability level: a higher level is stricter). The vertical axis counts the people removed. There is no course value, because this is an alternative method.

**Try this.**

- Move the slider to **0.99**. Many more people are removed.
- Move it to **0.9999**. The count comes close to the course rule.

**What you should see, and why.** About 1 in 100 people of a perfectly normal group lies beyond the 0.99 point, so this cutoff flags normal Europeans. Stricter cutoffs keep mainly the distant people.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** If you prefer a distance method, choose its cutoff before you see results and report it.

**Key idea:** A statistical cutoff flags some normal people, so check who is flagged.

```{r s5-6_thresholds, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. Nothing here changes the files of step 5.6. The package MASS comes with R.
# 1. Read the scores of step 5.4 and apply the methods to the same samples.
metadata <- guided_table(file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38.psam"))
ref <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores"), ".sscore"))
study <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores"), ".sscore"))
result <- ancestry_outliers(ref, study, metadata$SuperPop[match(ref$IID, metadata$IID)])
# 2. Change the number of SD of the course rule.
sd_trial <- outlier_sd_counts(result, c(4, 5, 6, 7, 8))
sd_trial$course_value <- sd_trial$threshold == 6
# 3. Change the chi-squared quantile of the robust Mahalanobis distance.
mcd_trial <- outlier_mcd_counts(result, c(0.99, 0.999, 0.9999))
mcd_trial$course_value <- FALSE
sd_trial
mcd_trial
# 4. Plot the removed samples.
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); plot_threshold_trials(sd_trial, "Samples removed", log_x = FALSE); plot_threshold_trials(mcd_trial, "Samples removed", log_x = FALSE)
# Optional: add engine = "ggplot2" to plot_threshold_trials() to draw the plot with ggplot2 (install.packages("ggplot2") once first).
```
Plain PLINK 2 command: not applicable. R reads the score tables and calculates the distances.

The expected result of the trials:

Study samples removed by the course rule when the number of SD changes:

| Setting | Samples removed | Samples remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | 34 | 1,810 |
| 5 | 33 | 1,811 |
| **6 (course value)** | 33 | 1,811 |
| 7 | 33 | 1,811 |
| 8 | 33 | 1,811 |

Study samples removed by the robust Mahalanobis distance (alternative method):

| Setting | Samples removed | Samples remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.99 | 86 | 1,758 |
| 0.999 | 39 | 1,805 |
| 0.9999 | 34 | 1,810 |
</details>

<details><summary>Another approach (optional)</summary>
This optional box is not part of the main path. No later step uses it. It writes only to files that start with `s5-6_alt_`, so the files and checkpoints of the main path do not change.

The course rule is simple: a sample is an outlier when it lies more than six standard deviations from the European mean on any of the first four PCs. This box compares it with two other methods on the same samples.

**Robust Mahalanobis distance (MCD).** The Mahalanobis distance measures how far a sample is from the centre of a group, and it takes the shape of the group into account. The minimum covariance determinant (MCD) finds the centre and the shape from the most compact part of the group, so outliers cannot move them. A sample is an outlier when its squared distance is above the 99.9% point of a chi-squared distribution with four degrees of freedom (one for each PC), which is 18.47. We use `cov.rob` of the package MASS.

**Nearest 1000 Genomes group.** This method assigns each study sample to the nearest of the four reference groups (AFR, EAS, EUR and SAS) by Mahalanobis distance. A sample is an outlier when its nearest group is not EUR. It also tells where each outlier comes from.

```{r s5-6_alternatives, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. Nothing here changes the files of step 5.6. The package MASS comes with R.
# 1. Read the scores of step 5.4 and the group of each reference sample.
metadata <- guided_table(file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38.psam"))
ref <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores"), ".sscore"))
study <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores"), ".sscore"))
group <- metadata$SuperPop[match(ref$IID, metadata$IID)]
# 2. Apply the three methods to the same samples and compare them.
result <- ancestry_outliers(ref, study, group)
outlier_method_table(result)
# 3. Save a plot with a different symbol for the samples that each method removes.
plot_outlier_methods(result, guided_path(cfg, "5.6", "alt_methods.png"))
```
Plain PLINK 2 command: not applicable. R reads the score tables and calculates the distances. It does not change the genotype files.

Expected result. The table has one row for each method.

| Method | Samples removed | In common with the 6 SD rule | Only this method | Missed by this method |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6 SD rule (course) | 33 | 33 | 0 | 0 |
| Robust Mahalanobis (MCD) | 39 | 33 | 6 | 0 |
| Nearest 1000 Genomes group | 33 | 33 | 0 | 0 |

The plot marks the samples that each method removes. The samples that all three methods remove form small groups far from the European cluster. The extra samples of the MCD method lie at the edge of the European cluster, so they are not ancestry outliers. With a cutoff at the 99.9% point, about 0.1% of a perfectly normal group is flagged, and the method flags more than that here. This is why the course keeps the six-SD rule. The nearest-group method gives the same samples as the course rule and adds a label.

References. Six standard deviations on the first PCs: Price et al. 2006, [doi:10.1038/ng1847](https://doi.org/10.1038/ng1847). The MCD estimator: Rousseeuw and Van Driessen 1999, [doi:10.1080/00401706.1999.10485670](https://doi.org/10.1080/00401706.1999.10485670). Outlier detection in PCA of genetic data: Privé et al. 2020, [doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa520](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa520). Assigning people to ancestry groups with a reference: Privé et al. 2022, [doi:10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.11.008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.11.008).
</details>

<details><summary>Optional: deep dives</summary>

These optional boxes are not part of the main path. No later step uses them. They write no file in your results folder. The examples use simulated data, so the true answer is known. The first box of [step 5.1](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-1) explains why. They explain why the course removes ancestry outliers instead of only correcting for them. They do not repeat the boxes "Try other thresholds" and "Another approach" above.

#### Deep dive: why ancestry can confound the test

**Why this simulation.** Why correct for ancestry in a case-control study? Here cases and controls come from different subpopulations.

**How to read the chart.** Circles are controls, triangles are cases, from subpopulations A and B. No variant has a true effect, so every small p-value is false. Lambda ([Lambda GC](../docs/glossary.md#lambda-gc)) is 1 when tests are well calibrated and above 1 when p-values are too small. The table also gives the share of tests with p below 0.05 (about 5% is right).

{{example:confounding}}

**Try this.**

- Move the **Share of cases from B** slider to **0.5**. Cases and controls have the same mix, and lambda is close to 1.
- Move it to **0.9**. Lambda without PCs is high. With PC1 as a covariate it stays close to 1.
- Move it to **0.7**. The inflation is in between.

**What you should see, and why.** Allele frequencies differ between A and B. If cases come more often from B, a variant that marks B looks linked to the disease. PC1 carries the A-B difference, so as a covariate it removes the false link.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** [Step 6.2](module_06_association.Rmd#step-6-2) adds PCs as covariates. [Step 7.1](module_07_plots_and_reporting.Rmd#step-7-1) checks lambda of your scan, and [step 7.7](module_07_plots_and_reporting.Rmd#step-7-7) compares it with and without PCs.

**Key idea:** If ancestry differs between cases and controls, tests give false signals, and PCs that carry ancestry remove them.

**R code.** Change `case_share_b` and run the chunk again.

```{r s5-6_dd_confounding, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. Nothing here changes your results folder. This takes about ten seconds.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
# Change this share of the cases that come from subpopulation B (half of the controls come from B).
case_share_b <- 0.5
shares <- c(case_share_b, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9)
frames <- lapply(shares, function(s) demo_confounding_frame(s, seed = 5000))
demo_plot_panels(frames, paste0(shares * 100, "% of cases from B"), c("Controls", "Cases"))
# Lambda and the share of tests with p below 0.05, without PCs and with PC1 as a covariate.
round(t(vapply(frames, function(f) unlist(f$stats[c("lambda_none", "lambda_pc1", "false_none", "false_pc1")]), numeric(4))), 3)
```
**Quick check.** Why does PC1 as a covariate remove the inflation here?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

PC1 carries the difference between A and B. That difference is what links the disease status to the allele frequencies. Once the model knows it, the link disappears.

</details>

**Reference.** Price AL, et al. 2006. Principal components analysis corrects for stratification in genome-wide association studies. Nature Genetics 38:904-909. [doi:10.1038/ng1847](https://doi.org/10.1038/ng1847).

#### Deep dive: why a few far-away people matter

**Why this simulation.** What does a handful of far-away people do to the axes?

**How to read the chart.** Circles and triangles are two close subpopulations, A and B. Squares are distant people. The table gives how well PC1 and PC2 separate A from B (above 3 is clear) and the share of variance on PC1.

{{example:outliers}}

**Try this.**

- Move the **Number of distant people** slider to **0**. PC1 separates A from B.
- Move it to **5**. PC1 still separates them.
- Move it to **10**. PC1 now describes only the distant people, and the split between A and B has moved to PC2.

**What you should see, and why.** PC1 is the direction of largest variance. Enough distant people carry more variance than the difference between A and B, so PC1 turns towards them. The difference between A and B moves to PC2.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** [Step 5.6](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-6) removes people far from the European group before [step 5.7](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-7) computes the cohort PCs. Otherwise outliers could use up a PC. A far-away person may also be an error, such as a swapped sample.

**Key idea:** A few distant people can turn an axis, so we remove them before we compute the PCs that we keep.

**R code.** Change `outliers` and run the chunk again.

```{r s5-6_dd_outliers, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. Nothing here changes your results folder. This takes about twenty seconds.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
# Change this number of distant people and run the chunk again (the other panels use fixed numbers).
outliers <- 1
counts <- c(0, outliers, 5, 10)
frames <- lapply(counts, function(k) demo_outlier_frame(k, seed = 6000))
demo_plot_panels(frames, paste(counts, "distant people"), c("Population A", "Population B", "Distant people"))
# How well PC1 and PC2 separate A from B. A value above 3 is a clear separation.
round(t(vapply(frames, function(f) unlist(f$stats[c("outliers", "separation_pc1", "separation_pc2")]), numeric(3))), 2)
```
**Quick check.** Why not keep the distant people and add more PCs?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

Extra PCs would be used up to describe a handful of people, and the ancestry differences in the main group would still have to be captured. A linear model with a few PCs also describes a few very distant people badly.

</details>

</details>

## 5.7 Cohort PCs and how many to include {#step-5-7}

We plot the variation each explains and save a complete checked starting point for module 6.", "student_plink_options": [{"label": "select common sites with weaker correlations", "options": [{"name": "--pfile", "explanation": "Reads the retained study genotype files s5-6_state.pgen, .pvar and .psam from the results folder."}, {"name": "--chr", "explanation": "Uses only chromosomes 1 to 22, the autosomes."}, {"name": "--maf", "explanation": "Keeps sites whose less common allele has a frequency of at least 5%."}, {"name": "--exclude", "explanation": "Leaves out sites within the regions listed in s3-4_high_ld.bed0, where distant sites can carry similar genetic information.", "modifiers": [{"name": "bed0", "explanation": "Reads DNA regions in the BED way: the start of each region is counted from 0 and its end is not included."}]}, {"name": "--indep-pairwise", "explanation": "Selects sites with weaker correlations within windows of 200 kb (200,000 DNA bases).
