### What we do

Calculate new PCs in the retained study cohort, look at the eigenvalues and save the full state.

### Why

The reference axes describe broad differences between world regions. PCs calculated inside the cohort can capture finer differences that matter for association. We prune the sites again, because the cohort has changed. We keep only common sites, which means a [minor allele frequency](../docs/glossary.md#maf) (MAF, the frequency of the rarer allele) of at least 0.05.

An [eigenvalue](../docs/glossary.md#eigenvalue) measures how much variation one PC explains. A [scree plot](../docs/glossary.md#scree-plot) shows the eigenvalues in order, from the largest to the smallest.

The long-range LD regions are the same as in step 3.4. The list follows the collection of Grinde et al. 2024 ([doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1011242](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1011242)). The course fixes the number of PCs at ten for the main model. We do not choose the number to get attractive p-values. Too few PCs can leave confounding in the results. Too many PCs can reduce the precision of the estimates. In module 7 we compare other numbers of PCs as a sensitivity check. We do not use that check to search for the most significant result.

### You need

The retained cohort from step 5.6, and the list of GRCh38 long-range LD regions to exclude.

### Command

```{r s5-7}
# 1. Prepare the regions to exclude and the site selection output name.
regions <- guided_high_ld(cfg)
prune <- guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "prune")
# 2. Select common sites on chromosomes 1 to 22 with weaker correlations with each other.
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.6"), "--chr", "1-22", "--maf", "0.05", "--exclude", "bed0", regions,
  "--indep-pairwise", "200kb", "0.2", "--out", prune))
# 3. Calculate ten components within the retained study group using the selected sites.
report <- guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "pca")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.6"), "--extract", paste0(prune, ".prune.in"), "--pca", "10", "--out", report))
# 4. Read how much variation each component explains and plot these values.
eigenvalues <- scan(paste0(report, ".eigenval"), quiet = TRUE)
png(guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "scree.png"), width = 1000, height = 700, res = 130)
plot(seq_along(eigenvalues), eigenvalues, type = "b", pch = 16, xlab = "PC number", ylab = "Eigenvalue", main = "Retained cohort: first ten PCs")
# 5. Finish saving the picture and print its location.
invisible(dev.off())
cat("The plot was saved to ", guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "scree.png"), "\n", sep = "")
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
guided_snapshot(cfg, "5.7", guided_path(cfg, "5.6"), 1811, 238513, parent = "5.6")
file.copy(paste0(report, c(".eigenvec", ".eigenval")), file.path(cfg$out, "checkpoints", "5.7"), overwrite = TRUE)
check_step("5.7", data_dir = cfg$out, work_dir = cfg$out)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-6_state --chr 1-22 --maf 0.05 --exclude bed0 results/guided/s3-4_high_ld.bed0 --indep-pairwise 200kb 0.2 --out results/guided/s5-7_prune --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-6_state --extract results/guided/s5-7_prune.prune.in --pca 10 --out results/guided/s5-7_pca --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--maf 0.05` keeps only common sites for the pruning. `--chr 1-22` keeps only autosomal sites. `--exclude bed0` skips the long-range LD regions listed in a BED file. A BED file counts the start of a region from 0 and does not include its end. `--indep-pairwise 200kb 0.2` writes the list of sites left after pruning, using windows of 200 kb and an r^2 limit of 0.2. `--extract` uses that list only for the PCA. `--pca 10` computes the ten cohort eigenvectors. `--pfile` reads the named genotype files in PLINK 2 format. `--out` sets the name of the output files. `--threads 2` limits the number of worker threads. `--memory 2048` sets the working memory to 2048 MiB.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

Ten cohort PCs, a scree plot and a complete saved state for step 5.7 with 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants. The first cohort eigenvalue is about 14. The signs of the eigenvectors can differ on your computer. This does not change how the PCs adjust the association. R saves the picture as a PNG file and prints its path. It does not show the picture in the console. To see it, open the file from the Files pane of RStudio (click the file name, then choose "View File").

<!-- verification_note:start -->The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks and the expected counts passed on Windows.<!-- verification_note:end -->

```{r s5-7_expected_figure, echo=FALSE, fig.alt="The first cohort eigenvalue is much larger than the subsequent nine; ten PCs are prespecified for association."}
if (requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE) && knitr::is_html_output()) {
  knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "scree.png"), winslash = "/", mustWork = FALSE), rel_path = FALSE)
}
```

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error message. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Should we choose the number of PCs by trying many models and keeping the one with the most genome-wide significant hits?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. Fix the main model before you see any association result. Report the sensitivity analyses openly.

</details>

### Files created

Pruning lists, eigenvectors and eigenvalues, the scree plot (PNG), the working state and the full 5.7 checkpoint.

<details><summary>Try other thresholds (optional)</summary>
This optional box is not part of the main path and does not change your results. The examples use simulated data, so the true answer is known ([why](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-1)). The box runs the association scan again with other numbers of PCs. It writes only files that start with `s5-7_alt_`, and it takes about three minutes.

**Chart: Number of PCs.**

**Why this simulation.** The course keeps ten PCs. Is that the right number?

**How to read the chart.** Each point is one number of PCs used as covariates. The buttons above the chart switch between the hits below 5e-8 and lambda. The diamond marks the course value.

**Try this.**

- Move the slider to **0**. Lambda is high, and there are more hits than at the course value.
- Move it to **1**. Lambda falls to near 1, and the hits fall to the course value.
- Move it to **20**. Lambda rises a little.

**What you should see, and why.** Without PCs, the ancestry difference inflates the tests and gives false hits. In this dataset one PC carries all of it, so later PCs only add a little noise.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** [step 5.7](module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-7) fixes the number of PCs before you see association results, and [step 6.2](module_06_association.Rmd#step-6-2) uses them. Fix the number first. Do not choose it to get attractive p-values.

**Key idea:** Choose the number of PCs before you look at results, because here one PC already does the job.

```{r s5-7_thresholds, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. Nothing here changes the files of step 5.7. This takes about three minutes.
trials <- guided_pc_trials(cfg)
trials$trials
# Plot lambda and the number of hits against the number of PCs.
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(trials$trials$k, trials$trials$lambda, type = "b", pch = 16, xlab = "Number of PCs", ylab = "Lambda", main = "Lambda"); abline(h = 1, lty = 2)
plot(trials$trials$k, trials$trials$hits, type = "b", pch = 16, xlab = "Number of PCs", ylab = "Hits below 5e-8", main = "Hits")
```
Plain PLINK 2 command: the function runs `--pca 20` on the pruned list of step 5.7, and then `--glm sex hide-covar firth-fallback` once for each number of PCs, with the same options as step 6.3.

The expected result of the trials:

| Number of PCs | Hits below 5e-8 | Lambda |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 17 | 1.5273 |
| 1 | 8 | 1.0101 |
| 2 | 8 | 1.0136 |
| 3 | 8 | 1.0137 |
| 5 | 8 | 1.0150 |
| **10 (course value)** | 8 | 1.0157 |
| 15 | 8 | 1.0185 |
| 20 | 8 | 1.0183 |
</details>

<details><summary>Another approach (optional)</summary>
This optional box is not part of the main path. No later step uses it. It runs its own PCA with 20 components and its own association scans, and it writes only to files that start with `s5-7_alt_`. It takes about three minutes.

The course keeps ten PCs. Three ideas help to decide how many a study needs.

- **The scree plot.** PCs that carry real structure stand above a flat tail. The elbow between the two parts suggests how many to keep.
- **PCs associated with the outcome.** A PC that differs between cases and controls can confound the test. We test each PC against the disease. A PC with no association adds little.
- **The inflation factor.** We repeat the scan with 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 15 and 20 PCs and read lambda and the hits. Lambda should be close to 1.

A formal test also exists: the Tracy-Widom test asks whether an eigenvalue is larger than expected from noise (Patterson et al. 2006, [doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.0020190](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0020190)). We do not run it here.

Leaving out long-range LD regions before the PCA does not remove every problem. Grinde et al. 2024 ([doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1011242](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1011242)) studied people of mixed ancestry. Later PCs described small parts of the genome instead of ancestry, and adjusting for them gave false links through collider bias. A collider is a variable that two other things both influence. Adjusting for it can make those two look related. Excluding known regions did not solve it there, and LD pruning worked better. In our cohort the risk is smaller, because only PC1 carries ancestry. Still, check what each PC describes before you use it.

```{r s5-7_pc_number, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. Nothing here changes the files of step 5.7. This takes about three minutes.
# 1. Run a 20-component PCA and the association scans for 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 15 and 20 PCs.
trials <- guided_pc_trials(cfg)
# 2. Show hits and lambda for each number of PCs.
trials$trials
# 3. Show the first eigenvalues and the p-values of the first PCs against the outcome.
round(trials$eigenvalues[1:5], 3)
signif(trials$outcome_p[1:5], 3)
# 4. Plot the eigenvalues (scree plot) and lambda against the number of PCs.
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(1:20, trials$eigenvalues, type = "b", pch = 16, xlab = "PC number", ylab = "Eigenvalue", main = "Scree plot")
plot(trials$trials$k, trials$trials$lambda, type = "b", pch = 16, xlab = "Number of PCs", ylab = "Lambda", main = "Lambda")
abline(h = 1, lty = 2)
```
Plain PLINK 2 command: the function runs `--pca 20` on the pruned list of step 5.7, and then `--glm sex hide-covar firth-fallback` once for each number of PCs, with the same options as step 6.3. The covariates are Age and the first k PCs (`--covar-name Age,PC1-PC10` for ten).

Expected result.

| Number of PCs | Hits below 5e-8 | Lambda |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 17 | 1.5273 |
| 1 | 8 | 1.0101 |
| 2 | 8 | 1.0136 |
| 3 | 8 | 1.0137 |
| 5 | 8 | 1.0150 |
| **10 (course value)** | 8 | 1.0157 |
| 15 | 8 | 1.0185 |
| 20 | 8 | 1.0183 |

Only PC1 stands out. Its eigenvalue is far above the rest, and it is the only PC clearly associated with the outcome. Extra PCs do not help and add a little noise. The course keeps ten PCs as a safe default. For a real study, choose the number from the scree plot and lambda, and report it.
</details>

<details><summary>Optional: deep dives</summary>

These optional boxes are not part of the main path. No later step uses them. They write only files that start with `s5-7_dd_`. The files and the checkpoint of the main path do not change.

#### Deep dive: from eigenvalues to the scree plot

**The idea.** In the first deep dive of step 5.1, the variance on a line was largest for PC1. That variance is the [eigenvalue](../docs/glossary.md#eigenvalue) of PC1. The next PC has the largest variance that is left, and so on. A [scree plot](../docs/glossary.md#scree-plot) lists these eigenvalues in order. PCs that carry real structure stand above a flat tail. The tail looks like noise. The box "Another approach" in this step uses this idea, and it also tests the PCs against the outcome and repeats the scan with other numbers of PCs. This deep dive only connects the numbers to the idea of variance explained.

**R code.** The chunk reads the eigenvalues that step 5.7 wrote and prints the share of each PC among the ten.

```{r s5-7_dd_eigenvalues, eval=FALSE}
# Optional. Nothing here changes your results folder.
eigenvalues <- scan(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "pca"), ".eigenval"), quiet = TRUE)
# PLINK writes only the eigenvalues of the PCs that it computed, so these shares are shares among the ten PCs.
round(100 * eigenvalues / sum(eigenvalues), 1)
```

**What to observe.** One PC stands well above the others, and the rest are close to each other. The flat tail is what noise looks like. The share that each PC holds is the variance explained, in the sense of the first deep dive.

**Quick check.** Why are these shares shares among the ten PCs, not shares of all variation?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

PLINK reports only the eigenvalues of the PCs that it computes. The share of the total variance needs all the eigenvalues, which the course does not compute.

</details>

#### Deep dive: can one region take over a PC?

**The idea.** A PC should describe differences between people across the whole genome. Sometimes it describes one region instead, where long stretches of variants are strongly correlated. Step 3.4 leaves out a list of such regions. Here you calculate the PCs twice, without and with the list. A loading tells how much a variant contributes to a PC. The plot shows the absolute loadings of one PC along the genome. The code picks the PC for which most of the 200 largest loadings fall in one window of 5 million bases.

```{r s5-7_dd_loadings, eval=FALSE}
# Course check. This step needs project version 2026.5 or later.
if (!exists("requires_course_version")) stop("This step needs project version 2026.5 or later. Your project is older. Download the new version at step 0.3.", call. = FALSE)
requires_course_version("2026.5")
# Optional. This takes about two minutes. It writes only files that start with s5-7_dd_.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
state <- guided_path(cfg, "5.6")
# 1. Select weakly correlated sites without leaving out the long-range LD regions.
without_list <- guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "dd_without_list")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", state, "--chr", "1-22", "--maf", "0.05", "--indep-pairwise", "200kb", "0.2", "--out", without_list), quiet = TRUE)
# 2. Calculate ten PCs and the loading of every site, first without the list.
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", state, "--extract", paste0(without_list, ".prune.in"), "--pca", "10", "allele-wts", "--out", paste0(without_list, "_pca")), quiet = TRUE)
# 3. Calculate them again with the sites of the main path, which leave the list out.
with_list <- guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "dd_with_list")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", state, "--extract", paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "prune"), ".prune.in"), "--pca", "10", "allele-wts", "--out", with_list), quiet = TRUE)
# 4. Plot the absolute loadings of the PC with the busiest window.
first <- pca_read_loadings(paste0(without_list, "_pca.eigenvec.allele"))
second <- pca_read_loadings(paste0(with_list, ".eigenvec.allele"))
pca_plot_loadings(first, second, c("Without leaving out the long-range LD regions", "With the list (the main path)"))
# For each PC: the busiest window of 5 million bases among its 200 largest loadings, and how many loadings fall in it.
pca_local_peaks(first)
```
**Where the block comes from.** The simulated people are mosaics of real phased haplotypes from the 1000 Genomes project. The simulator does not add a block of strong LD on purpose. The block is inherited from the real haplotypes, and real genomes have long LD in the region of chromosome 6 that holds the major histocompatibility complex (MHC). So this is not a discovery. It shows what real genomes do, and why the list exists. The list of step 3.4 covers this region of chromosome 6.

**What to observe.** Without the list, one PC has a tall block of loadings in one place, which is drawn as orange triangles. With the list, the block is gone. The table shows the chromosome, the start of the window in millions of bases, and the number of the 200 largest loadings in it. A PC like this describes one region, not the ancestry of the people. This is why the course leaves the regions out in steps 3.4 and 5.7.

**Quick check.** Leaving out the list removes the block in this example. Does it solve the problem in every study?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. Grinde et al. 2024 ([doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1011242](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1011242)) found that leaving out regions found in earlier studies did not remove the problem in samples of mixed ancestry, and that LD pruning worked better there. The habit to keep is to look at what each PC describes before you use it.

</details>

**References.** Privé et al. 2020 ([doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa520](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa520)) found that some PCs of the UK Biobank describe complex LD structure and not population structure. Novembre et al. 2008 ([doi:10.1038/nature07331](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature07331)) describe how they removed regions with long-range LD, such as the inversions on 8p23 and 17q21.31, before the PCA.

</details>

## Module 5 recap {#module-5-recap}

- You compared the study with a GRCh38 reference subset of 1,062 samples.
- You kept 48,615 shared sites, and all of them matched on chromosome, position and alleles.
- You placed 1,844 study samples on the reference axes and drew the plot.
- You applied the six-standard-deviation rule and excluded 33 outlier records.
- 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants remain, with ten cohort PCs ready for the association model.

**Next:** module 6, where you run the association test and use these PCs as covariates.
